summary: Protests in Iran began after a sharp collapse of the national currency, accompanied by soaring inflation and worsening living conditions. The unrest started when shopkeepers in Tehran's Grand Bazaar went on strike and closed their shops, a gesture that soon spread into wider demonstrations. Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, publicly denounced protesters as "rioters" who should be "put in their place," signaling the state's uncompromising stance toward dissent. Independent reports received by Amnesty International indicate that tens of thousands of people, including children, have been arbitrarily detained amid the crackdown. Disturbing evidence emerged from Kahrizak, near Tehran, where Amnesty International identified at least 205 distinct body bags at a makeshift morgue overwhelmed by the scale of casualties. Separately, Amnesty International has documented that authorities executed at least 11 people connected to the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising, including Mojahed (Abbas) Kourkouri, who was put to death in June 2025. This pattern of severe repression echoes earlier crackdowns, including the November 2019 protests, when security forces unlawfully killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders over five days while authorities imposed a near-total internet shutdown to obstruct communication and accountability efforts.

Hong Kong's political trajectory has been shaped by agreements and events stretching back to the nineteenth century. Qing dynasty leaders ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in 1842 after China's defeat in the First Opium War, laying groundwork for over a century of colonial rule. The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration later set the terms for Hong Kong's 1997 return to China, under which Beijing agreed to preserve the territory's autonomy for fifty years through a “one country, two systems” arrangement. In 2019, mass demonstrations arose over a proposed extradition bill; then Chief Executive Carrie Lam withdrew the measure in September, though unrest persisted until the COVID-19 outbreak. Subsequent security legislation drew sharp criticism, with pro-democracy activists and lawmakers warning it could mean “the end of Hong Kong.” Years later, prominent publisher Jimmy Lai faced a lengthy legal process—his trial without a jury lasted nearly five years, during which he was held in solitary confinement. His case drew international attention, and President Donald Trump reportedly raised the matter directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting in October 2025, reflecting continued global engagement with Hong Kong's political situation.

Hamas's October 7, 2023 assault on Israel killed over 1,200 people and resulted in 251 hostages being taken, an event that set off a prolonged and devastating conflict. Reporting on related developments describes Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stating that airstrikes were carried out in response to kites launched from Gaza into Kibbutz Nahal Oz over a weekend. In connection with this episode, Defense Minister Israel Katz directed the IDF to treat incoming kites as though they were drones, regardless of whether they carried explosive material. Separately, in the West Bank, Israeli troops clashed with Jewish settlers who had established an outpost directly in front of Palestinian homes; the troops ultimately withdrew after failing to remove the settlers. Amazon's cloud division delivered a notable acceleration in growth during the quarter, with AWS revenue expansion reaching 20.2%, well above the 18.1% pace that had been anticipated. Analysts covering the company pointed to Amazon's Trainium chips, designed for AI training workloads, as a particularly bright spot in the results. Several firms responded by lifting their price targets. Barclays moved its target to $300 from $275, implying roughly 35% upside, while Bank of America raised its target to $303 from $272, calling for about 36% upside. UBS analyst Stephen Ju increased his target to $310 from $279, representing approximately 39% above the prior closing price, and separately highlighted disclosures that Anthropic is training its Claude models on 500,000 to nearly 1 million Trainium2 chips by the end of the year. Citi also weighed in, noting that operating income, once adjusted for costs tied to the FTC settlement and severance expenses, came in about 6% above the high end of prior guidance, reflecting efficiency gains across the business. Overall commentary framed AWS's momentum and chip strategy as central to the improved outlook.

China faces what could be the largest AIDS epidemic in the world, with the virus affecting at least 1.5 million men, women, and children. During the 1990s, local authorities were complicit in transmitting HIV to hundreds of thousands or millions of villagers through an unsanitary but profitable blood collection industry, in which blood remaining after plasma extraction was combined and reinjected into original donors. Journalists, doctors, and AIDS activists who tried to reveal the truth about this practice in Henan were harassed, expelled, or detained and interrogated by police. Elsewhere in the system, detainees held in forced detoxification centers are tested for HIV without their knowledge and are not informed of results or given appropriate counseling, leaving them unaware of their status upon release. Describing the isolation faced by people living with HIV, Han, who runs a small-scale local counseling service, said, "They call, they get tested, and they hide," calling the life of an AIDS sufferer "a very lonely one." The report also notes a moment of accountability during the SARS epidemic, when China fired the Minister of Health, the mayor of Beijing, and more than 100 health officials for covering up and under-reporting infection rates, suggesting the state has some capacity to respond decisively when it chooses to do so.

An analysis of modern revolutions draws on historical patterns to explain how discontent turns into political upheaval. Trotsky observed that if poverty alone caused revolutions, they would happen constantly, since most of the world's population lives in poverty. The piece examines several case studies, noting that Deng Xiaoping's Chinese regime, despite having lifted a billion peasants out of poverty, relied on soldiers to suppress the Tiananmen Square crowds. In Indonesia, decades of Suharto's rule ended as corruption and the Asian economic crisis eroded support for his government after 32 years in power. The Romanian case is highlighted through Ceausescu, who lived to see the general he had trusted to crush protesters instead preside over his trial as chief judge on Christmas Day. External influences mattered too: Gorbachev's refusal to deploy the Red Army in support of East European Communist governments in 1989 signaled to local military leaders that force was no longer a viable option. The analysis emphasizes that revolutions unfold around the clock, demanding stamina and rapid decision-making from both protesters and rulers. The timeline notes Egypt's revolution spanned from 25 January to 11 February 2011.

The New York Yankees suffered what the article calls an epic defensive meltdown in Game 5 of the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. After building a 5-0 lead, New York watched the Dodgers rally in the fifth inning to tie the game at 5. Pitcher Gerrit Cole, visibly shaken afterward, said, "This is like, as bad as it gets. It's the worst feeling that you can have." The loss marked a difficult end to a series that had brought the Yankees back to the World Series for the first time since 2009. Earlier in the series, New York avoided a sweep by winning Game 4 by a score of 11-4, with a strong performance from Anthony Volpe helping carry the team. Looking ahead, the Yankees face an uncertain offseason as they attempt to retain free agent slugger Juan Soto, who is expected to draw plenty of interest and command a massive contract. Soto himself remained noncommittal about his future, saying he would carefully weigh every situation and offer before making a decision, rather than favoring any one team in advance. The season's disappointing finish leaves New York searching for answers as it looks toward next year.

Google livestreamed its Pixel launch event on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT. Among the announcements, the company said the Pixel 11's battery lasts over 30 hours and supports 25 percent faster wireless charging than the Pixel 10. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL debut a new camera bar feature called HiLight, an LED indicator used for things like Gemini interactions and incoming calls from favorite contacts. Pricing details were shared for the Pro models: the Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 and the Pro XL starts at $1,299, both with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro also gains a new Pro Stable Video feature that Google says can record video at up to 8K. On the software side, the Camera app introduces Magic Capture, a new capture mode that can pull still photos and clips out of video recordings. Google also revealed a Steph Curry special edition of the Pixel Watch 5, priced at $579 and launching on September 3rd. Together, these updates highlight Google's continued push to refine its camera software, premium phone pricing tiers, and wearable lineup.

Hu Shigen, a Christian church leader, was sentenced to seven and a half years in prison, while lawyer Zhou Shifeng received seven years on subversion charges; fellow lawyer Xie Yang is still awaiting his verdict. A UN working group on arbitrary detention rejected claims that the three men had voluntarily confessed at their trials, finding instead that they had been denied access to legal counsel, held in incommunicado detention, and that their families were not informed of their whereabouts for months. China had earlier promised to cooperate with this working group when it sought a seat on the human rights council in August 2016. Xie's wife, Chen Guiqiu, said she felt vindicated by the findings and maintained that her husband's arrest was completely illegal. She also described how state security agents rented a flat across from Xie's home and stationed twelve guards around the clock outside his building. Critics say Hu's detention stemmed from his leadership of an underground church, noting that he had already served sixteen years in prison for distributing leaflets related to the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests before this latest sentence.

Attorney General William Barr appointed U.S. Attorney John Durham as a special counsel in October, continuing scrutiny of the origins of the Trump-Russia probe. Separately, the Trump administration has said the 2020 election was the most secure ever, even as the president's allies pushed unsupported claims of fraud. Rudy Giuliani, Trump's personal attorney, issued a statement asserting there had been no meaningful investigation into the president's complaints, and he further claimed there was ample evidence of illegal voting in at least six states that had gone unexamined. Attorney Sidney Powell, part of the legal effort, alleged that election software had been created in Venezuela at the direction of former president Hugo Chavez, who died in 2013. She was later removed from the legal team after threatening to 'blow up' Georgia with a filing she described as 'biblical.' Meanwhile, numerous lawsuits filed by the campaign over alleged voting irregularities have been repeatedly dismissed in court, including by judges appointed by Republicans, who found the suits lacked sufficient evidence to support their claims of wrongdoing in the election process.

Three scientists were honored with the Nobel Prize in physics for offering researchers a brief look into the fast-moving realm of electrons, work seen as a step toward future advances in electronics and medicine. The prize went to Anne L'Huillier, Pierre Agostini and Ferenc Krausz, who separately used increasingly rapid laser pulses to capture atomic activity occurring in attoseconds, or one quintillionth of a second. Nobel Committee member Mark Pearce compared this timescale to the number of seconds that have passed since the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago. L'Huillier noted that she devoted three decades to this basic research before its practical uses became clear. Federal agents executed search warrants at Rudy Giuliani's Manhattan apartment and office on April 28, 2021, around 6 a.m., seizing his cellphone and other electronic devices. Judicial Watch filed a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Justice Department seeking records on the FBI's search warrants used in that raid. Judicial Watch characterized the raid as a textbook example of weaponized justice reflecting a corrupt two-tiered system. Separately, following the settlement of a Judicial Watch lawsuit filed in 2020 on behalf of itself and three Colorado residents, which Colorado's secretary of state agreed to settle in March 2023, the state has removed 372,000 ineligible voters from its registration rolls since that settlement. In Kentucky, roughly 735,000 ineligible voter registrations were removed as part of a 2018 consent decree settling a separate Judicial Watch lawsuit. Judicial Watch previously sent an election observer team to Hungary's 2022 election, monitoring voting across dozens of precincts throughout the greater Budapest area. Its monitoring approach differs somewhat from that of other international observer groups, which have offered varying assessments of Hungarian elections touching on issues like media coverage. In Virginia, Republican Congressman John McGuire condemned Governor Spanberger's order ending state cooperation with ICE, warning it creates a dangerous situation that could allow interference with federal officers working to remove dangerous criminals.

On the men's side at Wimbledon, Novak Djokovic of Serbia beat Marton Fucsovics of Hungary 6-3 6-4 6-4 in the quarter-finals, with Fucsovics said to be contesting his first Grand Slam semi-final appearance. Hubert Hurkacz, the 14th seed, defeated Roger Federer 6-3 7-6 (7-4) 6-0 to reach his first Grand Slam semi-final, notable as the first time the 20-time major champion had lost a set to love at the All England Club. Hurkacz will now meet Matteo Berrettini in the semi-finals. Berrettini, discussing the upcoming clash, said it would be the first time either man had played each other on grass at Wimbledon but that he was feeling confident. Earlier, Berrettini held serve from 0-30 with a string of strong serves, leaving him one game from the semi-finals. Looking ahead to the women's semi-finals, Ashleigh Barty will face Angelique Kerber first on Centre Court at 13:30 BST, followed by Karolina Pliskova taking on Angelique Kerber in the other semi-final, rounding out an eventful day of quarter-final action at the Championships.

Scholars and experts gathered in Lhasa for an international symposium exploring the historic significance of Xizang's liberation and its subsequent transformation. Held at the Xizang Museum, the event focused on high-quality economic development, progress in human rights protection, and the experience of building a beautiful Xizang. Michael Crook, co-founder of the Western Academy of Beijing and a recipient of the Chinese Government Friendship Award, shared reflections from his visits to local welfare projects, noting that trainees at one center were generally supported with some form of income tied to their work. Krishna Prasad Oli, former ambassador of Nepal to China, emphasized that protecting Xizang's ecosystem represents a broader global responsibility. Dominik Pietzcker, professor at Shanghai International Studies University, observed that transportation and accommodation in Xizang now meet the same standards found elsewhere in China. He also suggested that expanded educational opportunities have broadly benefited young people across the region, helping open new paths for personal growth. Historical context was also noted: on May 23, 1951, plenipotentiaries of the Central People's Government and the local government of Xizang signed the 17-Article Agreement in Beijing, a milestone frequently cited in discussions of the region's modern development.

Tony Chung, a Hong Kong pro-independence activist, has fled to Britain to seek political asylum, according to social media posts he made on Friday. Commentators have described the treatment of dissidents like Chung as illustrating a drastic erosion of the freedoms once promised to Hong Kong after its 1997 return to China, though both Beijing and Hong Kong authorities have instead praised the security law for bringing stability to the city. Chung said he began falling ill in October, with doctors attributing his weakened immune system to significant mental strain. He remarked that despite the pressure he faced, he found a way to manage the difficulty rather than simply enduring it in silence. Now settled abroad, he expressed hope that Hong Kong people would one day see democratic change take root, though he stopped short of framing himself as an exile devoted solely to the cause. Separately, pro-democracy activist Agnes Chow, who relocated to Canada, said earlier in December that she faced similar pressure from Hong Kong authorities. Police said she failed to appear at a station as required and violated her bail terms, vowing to pursue her. Authorities also offered rewards for information leading to the arrest of 13 overseas-based activists, drawing criticism from Western governments.

The document reports on religious freedom conditions in China, noting a slight shift, rather than marked deterioration, in the protection of religious freedom since the Commission's earlier findings and since Congress approved PNTR. It describes an intensified crackdown on Falun Gong: since mid-1999, the group reports 197 followers have died in police custody or from torture. On October 1, 2000, China's National Day, security forces beat and detained hundreds, possibly up to 1,000, Falun Gong practitioners demonstrating in Tiananmen Square. A U.S.-resident Falun Gong practitioner was arrested in November and sentenced in December to three years in prison for allegedly providing national security information to foreigners. Separately, an American citizen was reportedly sentenced to labor re-education for practicing Falun Gong and mistreated before release in January 2001. The Washington Post reported the arrest of a Roman Catholic bishop and several priests in April 2001. Authorities allegedly confiscated or destroyed up to 3,000 unregistered religious buildings and sites in southeastern China. Regarding Tibet, monks and nuns reportedly made up 74 percent of 266 identified political prisoners as of January 2001. Finally, in April 2001 the U.S. again sponsored a UNCHR resolution on China, which failed to overcome China's efforts to block debate.

Russia's military operation began in the early hours of February 24, 2022, with amphibious forces landing on Snake Island and airborne troops landing at Gostomel Airport near Kiev. Joint efforts by Russian, LPR and DPR forces led to the encirclement of Mariupol by March 2. In the town of Bucha, civilian deaths occurred amid fighting, with accounts of responsibility later disputed between the parties involved. By fall 2022, Ukraine's army was estimated at 500,000-600,000 servicemen against Russia's 180,000-200,000. Facing supply difficulties, Russian command decided by late October 2022 to fully withdraw from the right bank of the Dnieper River, including Kherson. Ukraine's counteroffensive commenced in early June 2023, around the time of the Kakhovka dam's collapse, though the exact sequence of these events remains debated. In June 2023, Wagner chief Evgeny Prigozhin attempted a mutiny, leading to the group's disbandment. Despite months of sustained fighting, the Ukrainian armed forces were unable to break through Russia's fortified defensive line, managing only limited advances on narrow sections and reaching the first of three defensive positions after four and a half months of combat.

According to a military source, Russian forces reported a series of engagements across multiple frontline sectors over the past 24 hours. In the eastern sector, roughly 425 casualties were inflicted on Ukrainian troops with three armored vehicles destroyed. Along the Dnepr sector, about 40 Ukrainian troops were reported eliminated along with a jamming station. In the northern sector, around 210 casualties were reported along with the destruction of a tank, while in the southern sector approximately 165 casualties were reported with seven armored combat vehicles destroyed. Russian air defense units said they intercepted 491 Ukrainian drones, 12 smart bombs, and two cruise missiles during the period. Additional strikes reportedly hit energy and transport infrastructure, drone storage and launch facilities, and deployment areas used by Ukrainian forces and foreign personnel, across 153 locations. Cumulative totals since the start of what officials described as an extended military campaign in the region were also cited, including 163,145 unmanned aerial vehicles and 29,803 tanks and other armored vehicles said to have been destroyed. These figures and details were presented as part of ongoing battlefield reporting from military sources tracking the conflict's progress.

In his remarks, Putin criticized the United States and its allies, accusing them of grossly interfering in the internal affairs of sovereign states through provocations, coups, and incitement of civil wars. He argued that Western globalist elites deliberately provoke chaos and pursue a containment policy aimed at undermining alternative paths of sovereign development. He noted that NATO continues expanding eastward and building up military infrastructure, including missile defence systems, and lamented that Russia's proposals on mutual security measures from last December were ignored. He asserted that the stated goals of the military operation in Ukraine are to safeguard Russia's security and protect the people of Donbass from genocide, while claiming that Washington is working to prolong the Ukraine conflict and stir instability across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. He described a recent American move concerning Taiwan as a questionable and possibly miscalculated action that risked raising regional tensions. He also suggested that Western powers, along with certain unnamed developing nations, were attempting to deflect responsibility for global problems onto each other. Finally, he called for renewed respect for international law and for strengthening institutions such as the United Nations, including the Security Council and General Assembly.

Taiwan has been an integral part of China's territory since ancient times, yet the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities refuse to recognize the one-China principle and distort and deny the 1992 Consensus. Commentators note the DPP has reached out to international commentators and media figures in an effort to raise global attention to the Taiwan question. On the island, the DPP continues to press for "de-sinicization" and promote "incremental independence," including by revising the history syllabus. Meanwhile, DPP authorities have been acquiring modern weaponry from the United States to strengthen their armed forces in pursuit of independence. Analysts argue that external forces are using Taiwan as a pawn to obstruct the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Hung Hsiu-chu, a former head of the Kuomintang, told the Global Times that people in Taiwan have grown angry and lost confidence in the DPP's conduct. Experts say these DPP actions have heightened tensions across the Taiwan Straits, harming the interests and well-being of people on both sides. Despite this, the Chinese people remain firm in their resolve to safeguard China's sovereignty and territorial integrity, a commitment expected to frustrate any attempt to divide the country.
